sources.title: Roman Observatory - NASA Science
sources.text:
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will help us solve some of the most profound mysteries in astrophysics, such as how the universe has evolved, its ultimate fate, and whether we are alone.

To make Roman’s sensitive measurements possible, the telescope will observe from a vantage point about 930,000 miles (1.5 million km) away from Earth in the direction opposite the Sun. At this special place in space, called the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point, or L2, gravitational forces balance to keep objects in steady orbits with very little assistance.

Roman’s barrel-like shape will help block out unwanted light from the Sun, Earth, and Moon, and the spacecraft’s distant location will help keep the instruments cool. The thermal stability of an observatory at L2 will provide a ten-fold improvement beyond Hubble in much of the data Roman will gather.

The amount of detail these observations will reveal is directly related to the size of the telescope’s mirror, since a larger surface gathers more light. Roman’s primary mirror is 7.9 feet (2.4 meters) across. While it’s the same size as the Hubble Space Telescope’s main mirror, it is less than one-fourth the weight. Roman’s mirror weighs only 410 pounds (186 kilograms) thanks to major improvements in technology.

The primary mirror, in concert with other optics, will send light to Roman’s two science instruments: the Wide Field Instrument and Coronagraph.

Instruments


Wide Field Instrument

The Wide Field Instrument is a 300-megapixel infrared camera that will allow scientists to look very far back in time. Seeing the universe in its early stages will help unravel how it has expanded throughout its history, which will hint at how it may continue to evolve.

Overview of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.


Name: Nancy Grace Roman was NASA’s first chief of astronomy throughout the 1960s and 1970s and is known as the ‘Mother of the Hubble Space Telescope’. The Roman mission was previously named WFIRST (Wide-Field InfraRed Survey Telescope) and was renamed in 2020 to the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope to honour Nancy Grace Roman. Planned launch: 30 August 2026 Mission theme:  Conduct a survey of the sky in near-infrared light. This will enable scientists to understand the nature of dark matter and dark energy and find new exoplanets. Status: Under development, following adoption by NASA in 2010   Partnership:  The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is a NASA-led mission to which ESA contributes as a Mission of Opportunity. Participating in these kinds of missions enables ESA and the European space community to take advantage of the opportunities that arise through partner agencies, providing an element of flexibility to the ESA Science programme.   European contributions:  Europe’s contributions to the mission consist of detectors (EMCCDs) for the Coronagraph Instrument, star trackers and batteries. Furthermore, ESA will provide time for downlinking data from the spacecraft to a ground station; to this end, ESA has built a new 35-metre antenna in New Norcia in Australia, next to an existing antenna that is also used by other ESA missions.


















The Roman spacecraft


Mission objectives: The Roman telescope will be a cutting-edge space observatory for in-depth studies of the Universe in infrared light. The telescope’s large field of view, fast survey speed, high sensitivity and advanced coronagraphic capabilities will allow astronomers to detect and study galaxies in the very early Universe, search for potentially habitable exoplanets and provide answers to some of the most pressing questions in astrophysics, such as the nature of dark matter and dark energy.The wide-field view of the Roman Telescope and the quick way in which the telescope can be re-oriented will enable astronomers to perform surveys very efficiently. A wide-field survey prioritises looking at a large part of the sky instead of looking ‘deeper’ into a smaller patch, as is currently achieved with the Hubble and Webb Space Telescopes.With one of Roman’s surveys, scientists will look outside of the plane of our galaxy’s disc in search of supernovas. Supernovas shine brightly and are visible from enormous distances. They are like signposts in the Universe. Astronomers use them to measure cosmic distances. These measurements reveal how fast the Universe is expanding and allow astronomers to determine a value known as the Hubble constant.In another Roman survey, scientists will look towards the centre of our galaxy and monitor the intensity of light coming from millions of stars over time. They could discover over 1200 exoplanets through their microlensing signature and more than 100 000 exoplanets through the more standard transit method. The transit method looks for the periodical dimming of starlight as a planet repeatedly crosses in front of its host star.
















Detecting exoplanets with microlensing


Microlensing events occur when the light from distant stars is altered due to the mass of closer stars. All massive objects passing in front of a distant star bend the star’s light due to their gravitational field, creating a temporary increase in the brightness of the star. With Roman, astronomers will monitor the brightness of millions of stars over time. When two stars align closely along the telescope’s line of sight, the nearer start acts like a cosmic lens, magnifying the light from the background star. As the stars drift along their orbits around the galaxy, the alignment shifts over days to weeks, changing the apparent brightness of the more distant star. If the lensing star has an exoplanet, the brightness of the background star will show an additional peak due to the gravitational influence of the exoplanet.Apart from exoplanets, Roman will also study dark matter by looking at another type of lensing that happens to distant galaxies. Their apparent shape gets warped by small clumps of dark matter spread out through the Universe. This effect is called weak gravitational lensing. By studying the tiny changes in the shapes of millions of galaxies, Roman will help astronomers accurately map the distribution of both normal and dark matter across the history of the Universe.    Finally, Roman will use multiple methods to shine a light on the nature and evolution of dark energy, which seems to be speeding up the expansion of the Universe. Roman will map clustering of galaxies over time and space. Depending on the evolution of clusters through time, it is possible to test the effect of dark energy on them.  Roman’s infrared vision will study the light coming from thousands of distant type Ia supernovas which will help astronomers trace the expansion of the Universe over time.



What’s special?: Roman will survey the Universe with a much larger field of view than the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope or the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope.  This is useful for selecting targets for missions that cannot look as ‘wide’ but are able to probe ‘deeper’ such as Webb.    Roman complements ESA's Euclid mission by combining a larger telescope with deeper infrared observations over a smaller survey area. Together, the two missions will provide a more complete view of the Universe, with Euclid mapping vast regions of the cosmos and Roman revealing fainter objects and finer detail.Euclid has the larger field of view in a single pointing (0.53 square degrees, compared with Roman's 0.28 square degrees), while Roman combines its still exceptionally wide field with a larger 2.4-m telescope. This enables deeper observations, more sensitive infrared spectroscopy, and finer image quality over a somewhat smaller survey area.Roman is also equipped with a high-performance technology demonstration coronagraph capable of seeing planets a billion times fainter than their stars. The mission will use the coronograph to directly detect and characterise exoplanets. A coronagraph works by blocking out incoming stellar light so that fainter objects around the stars can be observed. Roman’s coronograph blocks this light by creating an ‘opposite’ wave. This opposite wave has peaks where the stellar light has valleys, and valleys where the stellar light has peaks. When the ‘opposite’ wave interacts with the light wave, they cancel each other out and only the light from possible planets and rings around the star remains.    Roman will advance and demonstrate the technology that will allow future missions to observe and characterise rocky planets in their star's habitable zone – the range of orbital distances where liquid water may exist on a planet's surface.
















Roman Wide Field Infrared instrument detector plane


Spacecraft and instruments: The Roman telescope has a primary mirror of 2.4 m and two instruments: the Wide Field Instrument (WFI) and a Coronagraph Instrument technology demonstration. The WFI is a 300-megapixel multi-band visible and near-infrared camera. The Coronagraph Instrument uses destructive interference to block out starlight in order to look for faint planets around them.  Journey and orbit: Roman is set to launch on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, USA. The space telescope will operate on an orbit around the second Lagrange point of the Sun-Earth system (L2).   Lifetime: The mission has a nominal lifetime of five years with a potential five-year extension. Mission facts:

In 2010, the Roman space telescope was put forward as the top priority for the next decade in astronomy by the United States National Academy of Sciences Decadal Survey Committee. The mission was proposed as WFIRST (Wide-Field InfraRed Survey Telescope) at the time.

Roman’s primary mirror is 2.4 metres in diameter, as large as the primary mirror of the Hubble Space Telescope.

The Wide Field Instrument will provide images of the same quality as Hubble, but its field of view is 200 times (0.28 square degrees) greater than Hubble’s infrared field of view.

Roman will gather up to 20 petabytes of data over the course of its five-year primary mission. This is the same amount of data as that of 10 000 000 HD movies all together.

The Coronagraph Instrument could be capable of imaging Jupiter-sized exoplanets in Jupiter-like orbits around their host stars.

sources.title: Where is the Roman Telescope in space?
sources.text: September 1, 20262 min read Add Us On GoogleAdd SciAmThis quirky spot in space is where NASA’s Roman Telescope will call homeThe Nancy Grace Roman Telescope is headed toward a Lagrange point, a critical position in outer space where gravitational forces behave in specific waysBy Mary Randolph edited by Claire Cameron GSFC/SVSThe Nancy Grace Roman Telescope just launched to space Sunday morning. The spacecraft is already more than 600 miles away from our planet—but it has many more miles to go.NASA’s newest space observatory is winging its way to a special spot in space called the second sun-Earth Lagrange point, or L2. This point is just shy of one million miles from Earth.From this distance, Roman will get to work: The telescope will be able to capture broad swaths of space in one image, giving astronomers never-before-seen views of stars, galaxies and other massive structures in the universe. Its survey will produce huge amounts of data and could solve several cosmic mysteries, with potential achievements ranging from understanding dark energy to detecting exoplanets—and finding some things astronomers don’t even know about yet.On supporting science journalismIf you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.It will take Roman about three months to make the journey to L2, but the trek will be well worth it. Lagrange points are crucial for space telescopes because, at these locations, the gravitational forces of Earth and the sun essentially balance each other out, keeping the spacecraft stable with minimal effort on its part. The pulls of our star and planet equal the centripetal force needed for a smaller object to stay in place.Matthew Twombly (graphic); Heidi B. Hammel/Shari Lifson/Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (content consultants)From L2, Roman and its soon-to-be neighbor, the James Webb Space Telescope, can orbit the sun without disproportionate pull from one direction or the other. In other words, they will stay put. Each of the observatories orbit a point in their halos.There are five sun-Earth Lagrange points. They are named after Italian-French mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange, who proved their existence in a paper entitled “Essay on the Three-Body Problem,” which was published in 1772.L2 is particularly ideal for telescopes because it’s close enough to communicate easily with Earth but far enough to get a clear, deep view of space. The first Lagrange point (L1) also hosts spacecraft, including solar and weather observatories; the other three points are uninhabited. Of the five Lagrange points, three are unstable, and two are stable. What that means is that spacecraft at the unstable points—L1, L2 and the third Lagrange point (L3)—need regular course corrections to keep them from drifting off into space.L2 offers a clear view of deep space and keeps the sun, the moon and Earth out of an observatory’s field of view. That means Roman will have the benefit of solar power and a lack of obstructions—giving it an unfettered look into the cosmos.Subscribe to Support Independent JournalismGreat science journalism requires human expertise, time, effort and creativity. sources.title: Roman Space Telescope live updates: NASA begins spacecraft commissioning process

2026-09-04T16:23:34.369Z
Roman finding its space legs
Animation of the deployable aperture cover on NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. (Image credit: NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab)
As it approaches the end of its first week in space, NASA's Roman Space Telescope is being preppared to begin its operational mission.Roman, which launched on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket on Aug. 30, and has already deployed its solar panels, high gain antenna, and deployable aperture cover, the large sunshade designed to keep stray bits of light from the telescope's view.

Mission teams also began the power-on process for Roman's Coronograph Instrument on Tuesday morning (Sep. 1). Now successfully up and running, the instrument will spend several weeks under the scrutiny of Roman's technicians as they perform tests to calibrate the corognograph before beginning science operations.

2026-08-31T22:29:54.998Z
Roman aces critical engine burn, fine-tunes trajectory


(Image credit: NASA)
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope performed an important 3.5-minute engine burn today (Aug. 31), fine-tuning its trajectory toward its distant destination. It was the first of two planned burns designed to get Roman to the sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2 (L2), a gravitationally stable point that lies about 930,000 miles (1.5 million kilometers) from Earth."The other, if needed, is planned for later this week, and Roman’s orbital insertion will take place approximately 100 days post-launch," NASA officials wrote in an update today. "Once in orbit around L2, Roman will only require periodic station-keeping burns roughly every 28 days."

2026-08-30T15:11:10.061Z
NASA, SpaceX celebrate & Trump calls in live during post-launch press conference

NASA's post-launch press conference has ended and it was not without some suprises. (Read our full launch wrap, with video and images.)NASA chief Jared Isaacman hailed the Roman Space Telescope mission team, as well as SpaceX's Falcon Heavy launch team, for smooth and successful launch.

"The telescope will provide a vast new atlas of the universe, potentially revealing more than 100,000 new exoplanets through its various surveys," Isaacman said. "So Roman will help us, as you've already heard, study dark matter and dark energy mysteries that may change our fundamental understanding of the universe."

Image 1 of 2

SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket launches with NASA’S Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope onboard from Launch Complex 39A, Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

(Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

Space.com Astronomy Editor Monisha Ravisetti wrapped the press conference with one last question about the science Roman could do.

In the middle of the press conference, Isaacman's phone rang and he quickly left the stage to take the call. It was from President Donald Trump."The president's excited about Roman," Isaacman said as he ran off stage.Isaacman returned a bit later and put Trump on speaker phone."I just want to thank everybody and congratulate you," Trump said. "Boy, it looked beautiful on television."That will be a wrap for our live launch coverage. Thanks for joining us and we'll see you at the next one!

2026-08-30T13:33:14.418Z
NASA post-launch briefing for Roman Space Telescope begins

Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Postlaunch News Conference - YouTube

Watch On

NASA's post-launch briefing on the successsful launch of the Roman Space Telescope is underway. You can watch it above. Read our full launch wrap, with video and images. Here's who is speaking today:
NASA Administrator Jared IsaacmanNicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA HeadquartersJackie Townsend, Roman telescope project manager, NASA GoddardJulie McEnery, Roman telescope senior project scientist, NASA GoddardDenton Gibson, launch director, NASA’s Launch Services Program, NASA Kennedy

2026-08-30T13:03:06.978Z
Relive the Roman Space Telescope launch ahead of press conference
As we wait for NASA's post-launch press conference for the Roman Space Telescope (that's set for 9:30 a.m. EDT (1330 GMT), let's take a look back at the stunning liftoff for the mission.You can see video of the launch above, but our Spaceflight Writer Josh Dinner captured this stunning view of the SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket carrying Roman as it crossed the sun during its ascent. Check it out!


A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket carrying NASA's Roman Space Telescope crosses the sun during launch from Pad 39A of NASA's Kennedy Space Center, Florida on Aug. 30, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)
See our full Roman Space Telescope launch wrap, with images and video.

2026-08-30T12:10:22.029Z
Roman Space Telescope deployed!

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is on its way to Lagrange Point 2 after a succesful deployment from the Falcon Heavy upper stage. Our wrap story will be posted shortly. A post-launch press conference is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. EDT (1330 GMT). We'll showcase that live here at start time.Roman separated from the Falcon Heavy on time at 7:57 a.m. EDT (1157 GMT), 31 minutes after launch, and will now begin commissioning its systems. That includes deploying its solar panels and preparing for a mid-course correction burn to reach L2, about 1 million miles from Earth opposite the sun.


(Image credit: NASA)
NASA expected to spend the next few weeks on commissioning Roman, essentially making sure all its systems work, then spend the next few months ensuring it is ready for its science mission. The first images are expected in January 2027.

Each Roman Space Telescope will have 300 million pixels, and NASA just launched an Adopt a Pixel campaign to let you sign up to "adopt" one for yourself. You can learn more about that here: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/adopt-a-pixel/Thank you all so much for joining us for our live launch coverage!

2026-08-30T11:54:55.585Z
Space Falcon Heavy aces final burn for Roman Space Telescope launch
The SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket carrying NASA's Roman Space Telescope just fired its engine for a second burn to refine its orbit ahead of spacecraft deployment."Nominal orbit insertion," SpaceX flight controllers reported.

This will be the final event before the Roman Space Telescope is released into orbit. Payload deployment is minutes away.

2026-08-30T11:38:48.575Z
Roman Space Telescope reaches initial orbit on SpaceX Falcon Heavy
SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket has successfully reached orbit with the Roman Space Telescope.The flight is now in a coast phase to prepare for final deployment about 31 minutes after launch (about 7:57 a.m. EDT, or 1157 GMT).

Both of the twin Falcon Heavy side boosters did land as planned, though SpaceX and NASA's pad video showed only one of the landings.

2026-08-30T11:33:33.327Z
Stage Separation! Falcon Heavy boosters to return to Earth


(Image credit: NASA)
Just over 4 minutes into flight for NASA's Roman Space Telescope, and a lot of things have happened in succession.The twin side boosters of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket separated as planned and performed their boost back burns to return to the Earth for a landing at the Cape Canaveral Space Forcce Station. The core first stage also separated from the second stage. It is being discarded on this flight.

The nose cone payload fairing also separated as the upper stage fired as planned.

2026-08-30T11:27:22.847Z
LIFTOFF! SpaceX Falcon Heavy launches Roman Space Telescope for NASA


(Image credit: NASA)
LIFTOFF! SpaceX's triple-core Falcon Heavy rocket just launched from Pad 39A of NASA's Kennedy Space Center to carry the Roman Space Telescope into orbit.This ascent should last just over 8 minutes, with the twin side boosters returning to Earth after separation for a landing at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station.

2026-08-30T11:22:08.786Z
Falcon Heavy ready for Roman Space Telescope launch
The SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket carrying NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is just about fully fueled for launch, with engine chilldown underway.Liftoff remains on track for 7:26 a.m. EDT (1126 GMT). From liftoff to deployment, the entire flight should last about 31 minutes, 31 seconds.

2026-08-30T11:16:20.074Z
Who was Nancy Grace Roman, namesake of NASA's Roman Space Telescope?
NASA's Roman Space Telescope is now 10 minutes from launch. So let's take a minute to talk about its namesake, NASA's 1st chief astronomer Nancy Grace Roman. You have her to thank for the Hubble Space Telescope.Here's why she's called the "Mother of Hubble."

2026-08-30T10:56:34.822Z
SpaceX now fueling 2nd stage of Falcon Heavy rocket for Roman launch


(Image credit: NASA)
Just minutes ago, SpaceX began fueling the second stage of its Falcon Heavy rocket with the RP-1 fuel for today's launch.All systems continue to perform well and there are no constraints for launch.

What is clear is that scientists are eagerly awaiting the Roman Space Telescope's observations of the universe. The space telescope is expected to be prolific."The scope is extraordinary," Roman senior scientist Julie Mcenery said during live commentary. "We will do a survey of our own Milky Way galaxy and find 20 billion stars. That would make it the largest catalog of astronomical objects that's ever been produced."We are now 30 minutes to launch.

2026-08-30T10:44:51.623Z
SpaceX begins fueling Falcon Heavy rocket for Roman launch


A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket carrying the Roman Space Telescope on the launch pad in Florida. (Image credit: SpaceX)
SpaceX is now fueling the first stage and side boosters of the Falcon Heavy rocket with the liquid RP-1 (rocket-grade kerosene) propellant it will need for launch. A report minutes ago confirmed that liquid oxygen, an oxidizer, is also beginning to be loaded.Weather concerns seem to be easing, with forecasts now predicting 70% "go" for launch.

2026-08-30T10:29:58.504Z
Roman is 70% go for launch!


NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope sits atop a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket on the launch pad on Aug. 29, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla — NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is now 70% go for launch this morning (Aug. 30). The observatory is on the launch pad sitting atop a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket and is set for liftoff in just under an hour at 7:26 a.m. EDT (1126 GMT) from Launch Complex-39A at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.Yesterday, a cloudy weather forecast pushed the launch probability to 50%. But thankfully, this morning the clouds have started to part and this probability has improved to 70%.

2026-08-30T09:39:03.272Z
Counting down to launch for Roman


NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope sits atop a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket on the launch pad. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla — After years of anticipation, we have finally arrived at launch day for NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Today (Aug. 30) at 7:26 a.m. EDT (1126 GMT), Roman is set to lift off from Launch Complex-39A at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.The mission will launch atop a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, sending NASA's flagship astronomy telescope out to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a stable orbital point approximately 1 million miles (1.5 million kilometers) out from Earth. As of yesterday (Aug. 29), there is still a 50% chance of favorable launch conditions. But at the launch site, everyone has their fingers crossed for a successful liftoff.

2026-08-29T12:47:32.093Z
Roman and Falcon Heavy standing on the launch pad


A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket stands at lc-39a for NASA's Psyche mission, Oct. 11, 2023. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla — With less than 24 until launch, SpaceX has raised Falcon Heavy with NASA's Roman Space Telescope at Launch Complex-39A ahead of tomorrow's 7:26 a.m. EDT (1126 GMT).Today, NASA will host a handful of press conferences and interviews leading up to the mission. At 9 a.m. EDT (1300 GMT), members of Romans' science team will provide a mission overview to discuss the telescope's instruments and discoveries ahead. A prelaunch press briefing will take place at 10:30 a.m. EDT (1430 GMT), which will provide the most up-to-date weather predictions for tomorrow's liftoff, as well as a status update on the rocket's progress in reaching the pad.

Both briefings will stream live on the Space.com homepage, as well as directly on NASA's website. Stay tuned for more updates as we track Roman's last day before launch!
T-24 Hours! Roman is slated to liftoff tomorrow at 7:26 a.m. EDT!NASA will host a Science Briefing today at 9:00 a.m. EDT to discuss the Roman Space Telescope mission followed by a Prelaunch News Conference at 10:30 a.m. EDT to discuss tomorrow morning's launch! pic.twitter.com/ASJs4EdQM9August 29, 2026

2026-08-28T23:33:38.793Z
Roman is go for launch!


The three first-stage boosters of the Falcon Heavy rocket that will launch NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on Aug. 30, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX)
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is officially "go" for launch! NASA made the announcement this afternoon (Aug. 28), after wrapping up the mission's Launch Readiness Review at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in Florida.SpaceX was part of that review, because Roman will lift off atop one of the company's Falcon Heavy rockets. Launch is scheduled to occur on Sunday (Aug. 30) at 7:26 a.m. EDT (1126 GMT) from KSC's Launch Complex-39A. You can watch it all live here at Space.com when the time comes.

2026-08-28T15:39:50.705Z
T-2 days until Roman launches to space


(Image credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio)
It is now under 48 hours until the scheduled launch of NASA's Roman Space Telescope. Liftoff from Launch Complex-39A is planned for Sunday (Aug. 30) at 7:26 a.m. EDT (1126 GMT).A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket will deliver Roman to Earth-Sun Lagrange point-2, a stationary sweet spot about 930,000 miles away that will keep the satellite in a persistant orbit on the side of Earth opposite the sun.

Weather Sunday morning is leaning toward favorable launch conditions, with a small chance of showers or thunderstorms during the 7 a.m. (1100 GMT) hour. Clouds and lightning will be the primary weather concerns, but conditions are expected to deteriorate more later in the day, giving Roman’s early-morning attempt a better shot of getting of the ground.If weather conditions worsen or Sunday's launch is delayed, another window opens Monday (Aug. 31) at 7:22 a.m. EDT (1122 GMT).

2026-08-26T18:09:48.905Z
SpaceX shows off Roman's Falcon Heavy rocket ride


The three first-stage boosters of the Falcon Heavy rocket that will launch NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on Aug. 30, 2026. SpaceX shared this photo via X on Aug. 26. (Image credit: SpaceX)
SpaceX just gave us some good looks at the rocket that will carry NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope to the final frontier this weekend.That launcher is a Falcon Heavy, whose first stage consists of three modified, strapped-together Falcon 9 boosters. In an X post today (Aug. 26), SpaceX showed off that trio, which are currently in the hangar at Launch Pad 39A at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The Falcon Heavy is scheduled to launch Roman — which will hunt for exoplanets and shed light on mysterious dark matter and dark energy — from Pad 39A on Sunday (Aug. 30) at 7:26 a.m. EDT (1126 GMT). You can watch the highly anticipated liftoff here at Space.com.

2026-08-26T10:40:52.661Z
Roman arrives at SpaceX hangar before launch


NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, encapsulated in its payload fairing, travels from the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility to the SpaceX hangar at Launch Complex 39A at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, ahead of mating to a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. (Image credit: Sydney Rohde (Rocz))
Roman is one step closer to space! NASA transported the new space telescope inside its rocket fairing from the Kennedy Space Center's Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility to SpaceX's hanger at Launch Complex-39A (LC-39A).The trip occurred overnight on Aug. 25, traveling in a caravan of vehicles to one its last Earthly destinations. Next, Roman and its protective fairings will be mated to SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket and undergo final fit checks and tests before rolling out to the launch pad.

A Launch Readiness Review panel will be held by NASA and SpaceX on Friday (Aug. 28), to make a final determination for launch readiness. If everything goes according to plan, liftoff will proceed toward the scheduled 7:26 a.m. EDT (1126 GMT) target on Sunday (Aug. 30).

2026-08-24T19:36:17.008Z
SpaceX seals Roman inside Falcon Heavy fairing ahead of Aug. 30 launch


(Image credit: SpaceX)
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is one step closer to launch. SpaceX has sealed the bus-sized observatory inside the payload fairing of its Falcon Heavy rocket, the company announced today (Aug. 24). Everything remains on course for Roman to lift off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida early on Sunday morning (Aug. 30).After launch, it'll take Roman about 30 days to reach its distant destination — the sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2, which lies about 930,000 miles (1.5 million kilometers) from Earth in the direction of Mars. After a roughly three-month checkout period, the scope will start observing the heavens — hunting for exoplanets and shedding light on dark matter and dark energy, among other tasks.

2026-08-24T11:45:15.308Z
NASA's next great space telescope is almost ready to leave Earth.

(Image credit: NASA/Sydney Rohde (Rocz))Roman has spent the last several weeks undergoing its final launch preparations at KSC. Technicians loaded the observatory with 290 gallons (1,100 liters) of hydrazine fuel on July 25, then attached it to its payload adapter in early August.Roman was recently encapsulated inside Falcon Heavy's payload fairing, and underwent a full launch-day dress rehearsal on Aug. 20. NASA, SpaceX and Roman mission managers then completed the mission's Flight Readiness Review on Aug. 21, formally clearing the observatory to begin its final launch preparations.Next, the telescope, encapsulated in its payload fairings, will be transported to SpaceX's hangar at LC-39A, where it will be attached to Falcon Heavy rocket before the it rolls out to the pad for launch later this week.
